22 OCTOBER 2026 · LEE C. STONEHOUSE

A joint is more than a hinge. Its movement can offer clues about whole-body flexibility, a useful part of the healthspan picture.

The Flexibility Score That Outperformed the Checkup: Why Your Joints Know Something Your Blood Doesn’t

Flexibility often gets reduced to one question: can someone touch their toes? That is a narrow view of a quality that involves many joints and movements.

In a 2024 prospective cohort study, researchers followed 3,139 adults aged 46 to 65 and examined a composite measure called the Flexindex. Over a mean follow-up of 12.9 years, lower Flexindex scores were associated with higher mortality.

That finding makes flexibility relevant to healthspan. It does not mean stretching is a proven way to extend life, or that the Flexindex is a better medical checkup. The study did not compare the score directly with blood tests or a routine health check. Its value is different: it draws attention to functional movement as one more measurable part of health.

THE SIGNAL BEYOND THE STRETCH

A body-wide score, not a toe-touch test

WHAT THE FLEXINDEX MEASURES

Twenty movements. Seven joint areas. One score.

The Flexindex combined 20 joint movements across seven areas: ankles, knees, hips, trunk, wrists, elbows and shoulders. Each movement was scored from 0 to 4, producing a total from 0 to 80.

That makes it a composite score, not a single stretch or isolated joint test. It captures a wider pattern of mobility across the body.

The study’s protocol matters. A hamstring stretch, yoga pose or score from a fitness app is not automatically equivalent to the research Flexindex. The measurement method and scoring need to match before results can be meaningfully compared.

Movement depends on more than a muscle’s length. Connective tissues also contribute to how the body moves and adapts.

WHAT THE STUDY FOUND

Lower flexibility was associated with higher mortality

The researchers compared participants in the lowest Flexindex group with those in the highest. After adjustment for age, body mass index and a health-status indicator that included chronic diseases and medication use, the lowest group had a 1.87 times higher mortality hazard in men and a 4.78 times higher mortality hazard in women.

Women in the cohort averaged about 35% higher flexibility than men. The estimates, particularly for women, need careful interpretation: the confidence interval for the female comparison was wide, which signals substantial uncertainty around its size.

These are group-level associations, not predictions for an individual. The study was observational, so it cannot establish that reduced flexibility caused deaths or that improving a Flexindex score would reduce mortality. Lower flexibility may reflect broader health, activity or functional differences. The authors called for intervention studies to test cause and effect.

The title’s comparison with a “checkup” is deliberately provocative, not a claim that flexibility outperformed blood tests. The study did not conduct that head-to-head comparison. A Flexindex can add a functional perspective; it cannot replace a clinical assessment or laboratory data.

WHY JOINTS AND VESSELS MAY TELL A RELATED STORY

Stiffness is not only about muscles

Flexibility is often discussed as a property of muscles and joints. But movement also involves connective tissues, and research has explored links between trunk flexibility and the stiffness of blood vessels.

In a 2009 study published in the American Journal of Physiology-Heart and Circulatory Physiology, poorer trunk flexibility was associated with greater arterial stiffness in middle-aged and older adults. Because the research was cross-sectional, it could not show which came first or whether one caused the other.

A 2020 meta-analysis in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health pooled eight controlled studies involving 213 middle-aged and older adults. It found that stretching interventions were associated with reductions in arterial stiffness measures. The authors also noted limitations, including the small overall evidence base and variation between studies.

Taken together, this research suggests that flexibility is worth considering beyond the range of a particular muscle. Connective tissue and blood vessels both have properties related to stiffness and elasticity. That does not make them the same tissue, or prove that a flexibility score measures vascular health. It does make the relationship a worthwhile subject for further study.

Blood vessels have elastic properties. Studies have explored how arterial stiffness relates to flexibility, without proving that one causes the other.

MAKE FLEXIBILITY MEASURABLE

Track the pattern, not a single party trick

A useful healthspan approach starts with a repeatable measure. For flexibility, that means looking beyond whether one stretch feels easier today.

  1. Use a consistent method. Compare like with like. The research Flexindex is a specific protocol, not a generic flexibility score.
  2. Look across the body. Notice whether movement is limited in one area or across several joint regions. A single test cannot provide that whole-body view.
  3. Track change over time. Repeat assessments under comparable conditions and interpret results alongside strength, balance, aerobic fitness and other relevant health measures.

This is a measurement framework, not a self-diagnosis tool or personal exercise prescription. Anyone with a concern about pain or restricted movement should seek suitable professional guidance.

Flexibility also belongs beside other aspects of physical capability. See the related articles on balance after 40, VO2max and healthspan after 40 and eccentric strength training over 50. Each offers a different view of how the body functions. None is a complete healthspan measure on its own.

The Flexindex combines 20 joint movements into a single score, giving a broader view than one isolated stretch.

LEE C. STONEHOUSE’S MEASURED METHOD

Lee C. Stonehouse became a personal trainer at 21 in California after competing as a bodybuilder. He wrote The Healthspan Extension Manual and built the 10-Tenet operating system to bring structure to the work of improving health and capability.

His own biological age was assessed at 47 against a chronological age of 63. That is a personal result, not a promise of what another person will achieve. It reflects the approach behind his system: measure, intervene, track and repeat.

A Flexindex is not a substitute for an independent, lab-verified biological age assessment. It is one possible functional measure within a broader view of healthspan. A well-rounded approach can combine movement and physical capability with biomarkers, recovery, nutrition, stress management and consistency.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

What is the Flexindex?

The Flexindex is a composite flexibility score built from 20 movements across seven joint areas: ankles, knees, hips, trunk, wrists, elbows and shoulders. In the 2024 study, each movement was scored from 0 to 4, giving a total score from 0 to 80.

Does poor flexibility predict a shorter lifespan?

A 2024 observational study found that lower Flexindex scores were associated with higher mortality during follow-up. It does not show that reduced flexibility causes earlier death, predict an individual’s lifespan or prove that improving flexibility changes mortality. The findings describe an association in the studied groups.

Can stretching improve arterial flexibility?

A 2020 meta-analysis of eight controlled studies found that stretching interventions were associated with reduced arterial stiffness measures in middle-aged and older adults. The evidence base was small and included varied study designs and protocols. It does not prove that stretching prevents cardiovascular disease or extends life.

Is the Flexindex better than a blood test?

The 2024 study did not compare Flexindex results with blood tests or routine checkups, so it cannot establish that the score is better. It measures a different aspect of function. Flexibility may complement other health information, but it is not a replacement for clinical evaluation or laboratory measurements.

Is the Flexindex the same as a toe-touch test?

No. A toe-touch test measures one movement, while the Flexindex combines 20 movements across seven joint areas using a defined scoring method. A toe-touch result can be informative about that movement, but it does not represent the full body-wide score used in the study.

THE TAKEAWAY

The Flexindex puts a number on a quality that is easy to overlook. In one middle-aged cohort, lower body-wide flexibility was associated with higher mortality. That is a meaningful signal, not proof of cause, a personal forecast or a substitute for a checkup.

Healthspan is best approached as a system. Measure what matters, include physical capability in the picture, and track change with methods that can be repeated.
